title: Germany: Historical & Regional Styles Outside the Judging Guidelines
attribution: German regional beers that no judging body catalogues, documented from German-language brewing publications. Figures here are NOT style ranges: no competition guideline defines these styles, so where a number appears it is one published recipe's target, transcribed from a named article and marked as such in the style's notes. Where sources disagree, the disagreement is printed rather than averaged. See Sources & provenance for each document's exact standing.

styles.name: Dampfbier (Bayerisch)
styles.impression: A Bavarian Forest survival: an ale worked warm and fast on Weissbier yeast, but built from barley alone. Malt-forward and lightly hopped, with the banana-and-clove signature of a Weissbier and none of the wheat — as its German source puts it, quasi ein Weißbier ohne Weizen.
styles.aroma: Slightly phenolic and banana-like, from a regular Weissbier yeast fermented warm at about 21 °C.
styles.appearance: Modern versions are deep gold to light amber. May be filtered or unfiltered. Historically a mitteldunkles — medium-dark — beer.
styles.flavor: Malt-forward and only very lightly hopped, finishing slightly phenolic and banana-like. Not heavy and not sweet.
styles.mouthfeel: Medium body, and notably low carbonation — wenig Rezenz — though the cited recipe finishes at about 3.5 g/L CO2.
styles.comments: THE NUMBERS ABOVE ARE ONE RECIPE'S TARGETS, NOT A STYLE RANGE. No judging body catalogues Dampfbier, so there is no measured minimum and maximum to publish. They are transcribed from a single bylined recipe in GradPlato, the editorial site of Fachverlag Hans Carl in Nürnberg — the house that publishes BRAUWELT and that published Horst Dornbusch's two German beer-style books. That article states Stammwürze 12 °P, Restextrakt 2.5 °P, 14 BE, 10 EBC and 5.1 % alcohol by volume; the gravities and colour here are those figures converted (12 °P and 2.5 °P to specific gravity, 10 EBC to 5.1 SRM), and the bitterness is given as 14-15 because the same page prints 14 BE in the recipe and 'bis etwa 15 BE' in its style description. SOURCES DISAGREE ON BITTERNESS: an unbylined German enthusiast article (Malzfreunde, 'Stile mit Geschichte' Folge 16) puts Dampfbier at 20-30 IBU and 4.8-5.2 % ABV. Its ABV band contains the 5.1 % used here, but its bitterness is roughly double, and it is a tertiary source under this project's rules, so its numbers are recorded as a conflict rather than merged. No malt bill is given above: the cited page's percentage column is internally broken (Pilsner 35 % plus Münchner 1 25 % sums to 60 %, not the stated 100 %, while its kilogram column is self-consistent and implies about 70/30), so it was not transcribed.
styles.history: Popular toward the end of the 19th century in the Bayerischer Wald near the Bohemian border, and brewed predominantly in summer. Lower Bavaria had little means of chilling a bottom-fermented beer, so brewers worked top-fermenting yeast warm and treated the result like lager. The name appears to come from the fermentation rather than any use of steam: an open vessel in vigorous primary throws large foam bubbles, and to the uninitiated each burst looked as though the wort were giving off steam. Contemporary lore holds that barley and hops in the impoverished Bayerischer Wald were not of the highest quality and that Dampfbier brewers had to beg fresh yeast from the richer Weissbier brewers nearby — which is no reason for a modern brewer to use poor ingredients. The style nearly vanished; a few breweries kept it, and it resurfaces occasionally as a revived historical style. Anchor's California Steam Beer answered the same lack of refrigeration independently and is not a relation.
styles.ingredients: Barley malt only — no wheat, despite the yeast. The cited recipe uses Pilsner and Munich I malt with Hallertauer Mittelfrüh at 4.25 % alpha for both bittering and aroma, an infusion mash at 67 °C for 30 min and 72 °C for 20 min, lautering at 76 °C, a 60-minute boil, about four days of fermentation at 21 °C with ordinary Weissbier yeast, then krausening with reserved wort and about two weeks of spunding near 0.5 bar. A separate tertiary source describes pale barley malt with small roast-malt additions, moderate regional hops such as Hallertauer, house top-fermenting strains and soft to medium-hard water.
styles.comparison: Effectively a Weissbier brewed without wheat: the yeast character overlaps, the grist does not. Distinct from California Common, which reaches a similar place from the opposite direction — lager yeast fermented warm, rather than ale yeast treated like lager.
styles.examples: Dampfbierbrauerei Zwiesel (brewed to a historical recipe); Hutthurmer and Lang-Bräu are named by a tertiary source as having kept the style alive.
